title: Stereochemistry & Chiral Drugs
summary: Understand why mirror-image molecules can act completely differently in the body.

lessons.title: Chirality & stereocenters

levels.kid:
Hold up your two hands. They look the same, but they are mirror images. Try to stack your right hand exactly on top of your left hand, palms down. It never fits perfectly! Scientists call things like this **chiral**, which means handed.

Some medicine molecules are handed too. A carbon atom holding four different friends can be built in a left-handed way or a right-handed way. Your body is full of handed parts, like a glove is shaped for one hand. So the left-handed medicine might fit and work, while the right-handed one might not fit at all, or might do something different.
levels.hs:
A molecule is **chiral** if it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, just like your left and right hands. A molecule that can be superimposed on its mirror image is **achiral**.

The most common source of chirality in drugs is a **stereocenter** (also called a chiral center): usually an sp3 carbon bonded to four different groups. Swap any two of those groups and you get the mirror-image version. The two mirror-image forms are called **enantiomers**.

A quick test for chirality: look for an internal mirror plane. If the molecule has a plane of symmetry, it is achiral, even if it contains stereocenters. If a carbon has two identical groups (for example two hydrogens, as in a CH2 group, or two methyls), it is not a stereocenter.

Why care? Proteins are built from L-amino acids, so receptors and enzymes are chiral. A chiral pocket can tell the two enantiomers apart, the same way a right-handed glove tells your hands apart. That is why one enantiomer of a drug may be active and the other weaker, inactive, or responsible for side effects. Glycine is the only common amino acid that is achiral, because its alpha carbon carries two hydrogens.
levels.college:
**Chirality** is a property of the whole molecule: a structure is chiral if it lacks any improper rotation axis (Sn), which in practice means no mirror plane (σ = S1) and no inversion centre (i = S2). A **stereogenic centre** is an atom at which swapping two substituents gives a stereoisomer. In drugs this is usually a tetrahedral carbon with four different substituents, but other elements count:

- **Sulfoxides** are stereogenic at sulfur (the lone pair acts as the fourth group). Omeprazole is chiral at its sulfoxide S, and esomeprazole is the (S)-enantiomer.
- **Quaternary ammonium** and **phosphorus** centres can be stereogenic. Simple amines usually are not usable stereocentres because pyramidal inversion at nitrogen is very fast at room temperature, unless the nitrogen is locked in a rigid ring or quaternized.
- **Axial chirality** arises when rotation about a bond is hindered, as in ortho-substituted biaryls (**atropisomers**).

A molecule with n stereocentres has at most 2^n stereoisomers. Fewer exist when internal symmetry creates **meso** compounds, which contain stereocentres but are achiral overall (e.g. meso-tartaric acid).

Stereocentres are created in drug synthesis, during metabolism (reduction of a ketone to a secondary alcohol, for example) and are sometimes lost (an acidic proton alpha to a carbonyl can let a centre racemize through the enol). Recognizing every stereocentre in a structure is the first step in deciding whether a compound must be developed as a single isomer.
levels.phd:
Formally, chirality is the absence of improper symmetry operations; the molecule's point group must contain only proper rotations (C1, Cn, Dn, T, O, I). This framing matters because 'stereocentre' is a local descriptor while chirality is global: meso compounds contain stereocentres yet belong to achiral point groups, and molecules with no stereocentre at all, such as allenes, spiranes, helicenes and hindered biaryls, can be chiral through axial, planar or helical elements.

The practical boundary between 'conformer' and 'stereoisomer' is kinetic. For atropisomers, LaPlante's classification uses rotational barrier and racemization half-life at physiological temperature: class 1 interconverts in under about a minute (treated as a single compound), class 3 has a half-life of years (develop as a single isomer), and class 2 sits in between and is the developability problem, because the isomers interconvert on the timescale of storage or circulation. Sotorasib is developed as a single, configurationally stable atropisomer.

Nitrogen illustrates the same kinetics: ammonia-type pyramidal inversion has a low barrier, so most tertiary amines are effectively achiral at N, whereas aziridines, bridgehead amines and Tröger's base have high enough barriers to isolate invertomers. Sulfoxides, by contrast, invert slowly at ambient temperature, so they are configurationally stable stereocentres.

In biology the chiral environment is the point. Proteins are homochiral (L-amino acids, D-sugars in nucleic acids), so the two enantiomers of a ligand form diastereomeric complexes with a target. Diastereomeric complexes have different free energies, which is the thermodynamic origin of enantioselective binding, metabolism and transport. Without a chiral partner, enantiomers are energetically identical, which is why achiral assays, achiral HPLC and NMR cannot tell them apart.
levels.expert:
At the bench, the first question about any new scaffold is 'how many stereocentres, and which are configurationally stable?' Count them before you commit to a series: every uncontrolled centre doubles the number of species you are really testing, and an assay result on a mixture is an average of compounds that may differ by orders of magnitude.

Pitfalls senior chemists watch for:

- **Hidden lability.** A stereocentre alpha to a carbonyl or bearing an acidic C–H can epimerize in buffer, in plasma or during salt formation. Measure configurational stability in relevant media early.
- **Atropisomerism you did not design.** Adding an ortho substituent to a biaryl or an N-aryl heterocycle for potency can quietly create class 2 atropisomers. Calculate the rotational barrier and check by chiral HPLC.
- **Metabolically generated centres.** Ketone reduction, sulfide oxidation to sulfoxide and hydroxylation of a CH2 can each create a new stereocentre in metabolites, which then need their own characterization.
- **Nitrogen.** Do not count simple amine nitrogens as stereocentres, but do count quaternized or bridgehead ones.

Regulators expect stereochemistry to be defined. Since the early 1990s the default has been to develop a single stereoisomer unless a racemate is justified, with an enantioselective assay, stereochemical identity tests and stability data.

Clinically, chirality explains real differences: one enantiomer of a beta-blocker carries most of the receptor blockade, and some marketed drugs are single enantiomers of older racemates. When reading a structure in a paper or label, look for wedges and hashes, an (R)/(S) descriptor, or 'rac' and 'rel' annotations; their absence often means the authors tested a mixture.

keyPoints: Chiral = not superimposable on its mirror image (like hands)
A stereocentre is usually an sp3 carbon with four different groups
A molecule with a mirror plane is achiral even if it has stereocentres (meso)
n stereocentres give at most 2^n stereoisomers
Chiral proteins distinguish enantiomers, so they can act differently
Sulfoxide S can be a stereocentre; simple amine N usually is not (fast inversion)

test.q: Which carbon is a stereocentre?
choices: A carbon bonded to H, OH, CH3 and CH2CH3
A carbon bonded to two methyl groups, H and OH
A CH2 carbon in a chain
test.explain: A stereocentre needs four different groups. H, OH, CH3 and ethyl are all different. CH2 has two H's, the carbonyl carbon is trigonal, and two methyls are identical.

test.q: A molecule is achiral if it has:
test.explain: A mirror plane (or inversion centre) makes a molecule superimposable on its mirror image. Stereocentres alone do not guarantee chirality (meso compounds).

test.q: Mirror-image stereoisomers that are not superimposable are called ___.
test.explain: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images, like left and right hands.

test.q: What is the maximum number of stereoisomers for a molecule with 3 stereocentres?
test.explain: The maximum is 2^n = 2^3 = 8. Symmetry (meso forms) can reduce the actual number.

test.q: Which common amino acid is achiral?
test.explain: Glycine's alpha carbon carries two hydrogens, so it has no stereocentre.

test.q: What is the term for a compound that contains stereocentres but is achiral because of internal symmetry?
test.explain: Meso compounds (e.g. meso-tartaric acid) have stereocentres but an internal mirror plane, so they are achiral.

test.q: In omeprazole, the stereocentre is located at:
test.explain: The sulfoxide sulfur has three substituents plus a lone pair and inverts slowly, so it is a stable stereocentre. Esomeprazole is the (S)-enantiomer.

test.q: Why are most simple tertiary amine nitrogens not counted as stereocentres?
choices: They invert (flip) rapidly at room temperature
They are protonated at pH 7.4, which locks their geometry
Their nitrogen is planar sp2 in its ground state
Their lone pair is not a substituent, so N has three groups, not four
test.explain: Pyramidal nitrogen inversion has a low barrier, so the two forms interconvert too fast to isolate.

test.q: Why can a receptor distinguish between two enantiomers?
choices: The receptor is itself chiral, made of L-amino acids
Enantiomers rotate polarized light, which the receptor detects
test.explain: A chiral receptor forms diastereomeric complexes with the two enantiomers, which differ in energy. Enantiomers share mass, boiling point and achiral solubility.

test.q: Chirality caused by hindered rotation around a bond, as in some biaryls, gives isomers called ___.
test.explain: Atropisomers arise from restricted rotation, an example of axial chirality.

test.q: Reducing a ketone (R–CO–R') with two different R groups to an alcohol:
choices: Converts the carbon into a planar sp2 centre
test.explain: The new carbon bears H, OH, R and R' (four different groups), so it becomes a stereocentre. This often happens in drug metabolism.

kidTest.q: Your left and right hands are...
kidTest.explain: Your hands are mirror images that don't stack perfectly. That's what chiral means.

kidTest.q: What does chiral mean?
kidTest.explain: Chiral means handed: something with a left and a right version.

kidTest.q: A glove for your right hand fits...
kidTest.explain: A right glove fits only the right hand. Your body's parts are picky like gloves.

kidTest.q: A carbon holding four different friends can be left-handed or ___-handed.
kidTest.explain: It can be built two ways: left-handed or right-handed.

kidTest.q: Can the left-handed and right-handed versions of a medicine do different things in your body?
kidTest.explain: Yes. One might fit your body's glove-like parts and work, and the other might not.

advancedTest.q: Which molecule lacks any stereocentre yet can still be chiral?
choices: Meso-tartaric acid with an internal mirror plane despite its two stereocentres
Benzene, whose aromatic pi cloud rotates under polarized light without substituents
A 1,3-disubstituted allene with different groups on each end
Ethanol, whose OH can adopt two transient rotamers around its carbon–oxygen bond
advancedTest.explain: Suitably substituted allenes have axial chirality with no stereocentre. Meso-tartaric acid has stereocentres but is achiral.

advancedTest.q: Under LaPlante's classification, which atropisomer class is the main developability problem?
choices: Classes 1 and 3 together, as both are hard to isolate
advancedTest.explain: Class 2 isomers interconvert on storage or circulation timescales, so neither a single isomer nor a fixed mixture can be guaranteed.

advancedTest.q: Why can't a standard achiral reverse-phase HPLC column separate enantiomers?
choices: Enantiomers have identical properties in an achiral environment
The UV detector absorbs equally from two enantiomers and cannot detect their separate peaks
Both enantiomers decompose on the silica support before the column can elute them
The enantiomers differ in molecular mass but have exactly the same hydrophobic retention
advancedTest.explain: Separation needs diastereomeric interactions; only a chiral stationary phase or chiral additive provides them.

advancedTest.q: A stereocentre next to a carbonyl with an acidic C–H can lose its configuration through which intermediate? (one word)
advancedTest.explain: Deprotonation or tautomerization to the planar enol or enolate erases the configuration; reprotonation from either face racemizes or epimerizes the centre.

lessons.title: R/S and E/Z nomenclature

levels.kid:
Imagine two twin toy cars that look the same but are mirror images. To tell them apart, you give each a name tag. Chemists do this with handed molecules. They use the letter **R** or **S**.

Here is the trick. Rank the four friends around the carbon from biggest to smallest. Point the smallest one away from you, like hiding it behind the carbon. Then go from biggest to next biggest to next. If you turn like a clock's hands, it is R. If you turn the other way, it is S.

For double bonds that cannot spin, the big friends on the **same** side get Z, and opposite sides get E.
levels.hs:
Because enantiomers look so alike, chemists need a precise label. The **Cahn–Ingold–Prelog (CIP)** rules give each stereocentre an **R** or **S** label.

- Rank the four groups by the atomic number of the atom directly attached. Higher atomic number = higher priority. For example: Br > Cl > O > N > C > H.
- If two attached atoms tie, move outward one atom at a time and compare the next sets of atoms.
- Orient the molecule so the lowest-priority group (often H) points away from you.
- Trace 1 → 2 → 3. Clockwise = **R** (rectus, right). Counterclockwise = **S** (sinister, left).

Double bonds use **E/Z**. Rank the two groups on each end of the C=C. If the two higher-priority groups are on the same side, it is **Z** (zusammen, together). If they are on opposite sides, it is **E** (entgegen, opposite).

Important: R/S does not tell you which way a molecule rotates polarized light. That is measured separately and written as (+) or (−). A drug label like (S)-(+) gives both facts.
levels.college:
**CIP priority rules** in full:

1. Higher atomic number at the first point of difference wins (isotopes: higher mass wins, so D > H).
2. For ties, build the set of atoms attached to each tied atom (e.g. CH2OH = {O,H,H}; CH(CH3)2 = {C,C,H}) and compare the highest atom first, then the next. Explore outward branch by branch until a difference appears.
3. **Multiple bonds** are expanded with duplicate atoms: C=O counts as C bonded to (O,O); C≡N counts as (N,N,N). So –CHO {O,O,H} outranks –CH2OH {O,H,H}, and –COOH {O,O,O} outranks both.

Assigning: with the lowest-priority group pointing away, 1→2→3 clockwise is R. If the lowest group is on a wedge (toward you), read the direction and reverse it. Swapping any two groups inverts the descriptor; swapping two pairs restores it.

**E/Z** applies CIP ranking separately to each alkene carbon. 'Cis/trans' describes the main chain or identical groups and can disagree with E/Z. Tamoxifen is an example: it is commonly called the trans isomer, but its CIP descriptor is (Z).

**Other descriptor systems** you will meet:
- (+)/(−) or d/l: sign of optical rotation, an experimental property with no fixed link to R/S.
- D/L (small caps): Fischer-projection configuration relative to glyceraldehyde, used for sugars and amino acids. Most L-amino acids are (S), but L-cysteine is (R), because the sulfur in its side chain outranks the carboxyl group.
- rac, rel, and R*/S* signal racemic or relative configuration.
levels.phd:
The CIP system is a hierarchical digraph procedure: each stereocentre is the root of a tree, branches are explored in order of precedence, and duplicate atoms represent multiple bonds and ring closures. Five sequence rules are applied in order: (1a) atomic number, (1b) a refinement for duplicated atoms introduced in the 2013 IUPAC recommendations, (2) atomic mass, (3) cis before trans (Z before E) for double bonds, (4) like pairs (RR, SS) before unlike (RS), and (5) R before S. Rules 3–5 resolve cases where constitutionally identical branches differ only in their own stereochemistry, giving pseudoasymmetric centres described by lowercase r/s.

This matters because the descriptor depends on the constitution around the centre, not on its spatial geometry alone. Two biologically equivalent molecules can carry opposite labels: replacing a substituent with a heavier atom (for example O-methyl to S-methyl, or adding fluorine) can flip R to S without changing the 3D arrangement. In SAR tables, labels can be misleading; overlaying structures is safer than comparing letters.

Axial chirality (biaryls, allenes) uses Ra/Sa or the helical P/M descriptors; planar chirality uses Rp/Sp. Atropisomeric drug candidates are usually labelled P or M.

Absolute configuration is determined experimentally, most definitively by anomalous dispersion X-ray crystallography (the Flack parameter), or by vibrational circular dichroism compared against computed spectra, or by chemical correlation to a known standard, or by derivatization methods such as Mosher ester NMR analysis. Optical rotation alone cannot assign configuration, and its sign can even change with solvent, concentration or temperature.
levels.expert:
Practical rules from the medicinal chemistry bench:

- **Assign on the drawing you will publish, and check with software.** Chemical drawing packages and registration systems assign CIP labels automatically, but they also propagate errors when someone draws a wedge on the wrong bond. Every new registration deserves a human look at the wedges.
- **Do not compare letters across a series.** A matched pair where one analogue is (R) and the other (S) may have the same 3D arrangement because a priority changed. Medicinal chemists talk about 'the same configuration as the lead' and overlay structures instead.
- **Know how configuration was established.** 'Absolute stereochemistry assigned by analogy' is a hypothesis. A single-crystal X-ray of the compound or a heavy-atom salt, VCD, or synthesis from a chiral pool material with a known centre are real evidence. Regulatory filings require a justified assignment.
- **Record what was actually tested.** Use 'rac' for a racemate, 'rel' or 'or1/and1' style enhanced stereo notation when only relative configuration is known, and isomer labels like 'peak 1' and 'peak 2' from chiral chromatography until absolute configuration is proven.
- **E/Z in drug names** matters for quality control: geometric isomers are different substances with different activity and must be specified and controlled.

In clinical pharmacology, labels like levo-, dex- and es- in drug names are shorthand for a single enantiomer (levo- and dex- refer to the sign of rotation; es- comes from the S descriptor). Knowing that 'levo' means rotation direction and not configuration avoids a classic exam trap.

keyPoints: CIP priority: higher atomic number at the first point of difference wins
Lowest priority away: clockwise = R, counterclockwise = S
Double and triple bonds count as duplicated atoms
Z = higher-priority groups on the same side; E = opposite sides
R/S does not predict (+)/(−) optical rotation
Most L-amino acids are S; L-cysteine is R

test.q: Which group has the highest CIP priority?
test.explain: Priority goes by atomic number of the attached atom: O (8) > N (7) > C (6) > H (1).

test.q: With the lowest-priority group pointing away, the path 1→2→3 runs clockwise. The centre is:
test.explain: Clockwise = R (rectus). Counterclockwise = S.

test.q: Which ranks higher by CIP rules: –CHO or –CH2OH?
test.explain: Duplicate atoms: –CHO is C attached to {O,O,H}; –CH2OH is {O,H,H}. {O,O,H} wins at the second atom.

test.q: When the two higher-priority groups are on the same side of a double bond, the alkene is ___.
test.explain: Z comes from German zusammen, together. Opposite sides = E (entgegen).

test.q: If the lowest-priority group points toward you (on a wedge) and 1→2→3 appears clockwise, the true descriptor is:
test.explain: Viewing from the wrong side reverses the apparent direction, so clockwise from the front means S.

test.q: What does the (+) in (S)-(+)-drug tell you?
choices: It is a racemic mixture containing equal amounts of the R and S isomers
It has a positive formal charge at physiological pH because of its nitrogen
It is the eutomer, the more potent enantiomer at its target
test.explain: (+) is the experimental sign of optical rotation. It is independent of the R/S descriptor.

test.q: What is the CIP descriptor (R or S) of L-cysteine?
test.explain: The CH2SH group outranks COOH because S has a higher atomic number than O, so L-cysteine is R even though most L-amino acids are S.

test.q: Rank these for CIP priority: –Br, –Cl, –OH, –CH3
test.explain: Atomic numbers: Br 35, Cl 17, O 8, C 6.

test.q: Swapping any two groups on a stereocentre ___ its R/S descriptor.
test.explain: One swap gives the mirror-image configuration, so R becomes S. Two swaps restore it.

test.q: Tamoxifen is often called the 'trans' isomer. Its CIP descriptor is:
test.explain: Cis/trans describes the arrangement of particular groups; CIP E/Z ranks all groups by priority. For tamoxifen the two disagree: it is (Z).

test.q: What letter does the Latin word 'sinister' (left) give as a stereodescriptor?
test.explain: S = sinister (counterclockwise); R = rectus (clockwise).

kidTest.q: Chemists give handed molecules a name tag. Which letters do they use?
kidTest.explain: They use R or S.

kidTest.q: To name it, the smallest friend should point...
kidTest.explain: Hide the smallest friend behind the carbon, pointing away.

kidTest.q: If you go around like a clock's hands, the name is...
kidTest.explain: Clockwise means R.

kidTest.q: Big friends on the same side of a double bond get the letter ___.
kidTest.explain: Same side = Z. Opposite sides = E.

kidTest.q: Opposite sides of a double bond get the letter...
kidTest.explain: Opposite sides = E.

advancedTest.q: Replacing an –OCH3 group with –SCH3 on a stereocentre's neighbor, without moving any atoms in space, can:
choices: Flip the descriptor from R to S because priorities change
Leave the descriptor unchanged because the 3D shape is fixed
Erase the stereocentre by replacing O with S nearby
Force all stereocentres in the molecule to become S
advancedTest.explain: S outranks O, so the priority order can change and the label can flip even though the 3D arrangement is identical.

advancedTest.q: Which method most definitively assigns absolute configuration?
choices: Optical rotation compared with an R-configured analogue
Melting point measured on a pure enantiomer
advancedTest.explain: Anomalous dispersion X-ray (Flack parameter) gives absolute configuration. Rotation sign cannot assign configuration.

advancedTest.q: What lowercase descriptors mark a pseudoasymmetric centre? (two letters, e.g. x/y)
advancedTest.explain: Pseudoasymmetric centres bear two constitutionally identical but enantiomorphic ligands and are labelled with lowercase r or s.

advancedTest.q: Which descriptor pair is commonly used for axially chiral atropisomers?
advancedTest.explain: Helical P/M (or Ra/Sa) describes axial chirality in hindered biaryls.

lessons.title: Enantiomers, diastereomers & racemates

levels.kid:
Molecules can come in look-alike versions. Some are perfect mirror twins, like your left and right shoes. These are called **enantiomers**. Mirror twins are the same in almost every way. They weigh the same and melt at the same heat.

Other look-alikes are not mirror twins. They are more like cousins: similar, but a bit different all over. These are called **diastereomers**, and they really do behave differently.

When a medicine is made as a 50-50 mix of left and right twins, that mix is called a **racemate**. Sometimes scientists sort the twins so the medicine has only the helpful one.
levels.hs:
Molecules with the same atoms connected in the same order but arranged differently in space are **stereoisomers**. There are two kinds.

- **Enantiomers** are non-superimposable mirror images. Every stereocentre is inverted (R becomes S everywhere). In a non-chiral setting they have identical properties: same melting point, boiling point, solubility and NMR spectrum. They differ only in how they rotate plane-polarized light (equal amounts, opposite directions) and in how they interact with other chiral things, such as receptors and enzymes.
- **Diastereomers** are stereoisomers that are not mirror images. This needs at least two stereocentres (or a double bond, since E/Z isomers are diastereomers). If a molecule is (R,R), its enantiomer is (S,S), and its diastereomers are (R,S) and (S,R). Diastereomers have different physical properties, so they can be separated by ordinary methods like crystallization or normal chromatography.

A **racemate** (racemic mixture) is a 50:50 mix of two enantiomers. It shows no optical rotation because the rotations cancel. Many older drugs are sold as racemates, for example ibuprofen and the beta-blocker propranolol.
levels.college:
Stereoisomers divide into **enantiomers** (mirror-related) and **diastereomers** (everything else, including E/Z isomers). For a molecule with stereocentres, changing every centre gives the enantiomer; changing some but not all gives a diastereomer. **Epimers** are diastereomers that differ at exactly one stereocentre (glucose and galactose differ at C4); **anomers** are epimers at the anomeric carbon of a cyclic sugar.

Purity terms:
- **Enantiomeric excess**: ee = |%major − %minor|. A 95:5 mixture has 90% ee.
- **Diastereomeric ratio** (dr) describes diastereomer mixtures.
- **Racemate**: 0% ee, written rac- or (±).

**Getting single enantiomers:**
- **Chiral pool**: start from cheap natural chiral materials (amino acids, sugars, terpenes).
- **Resolution**: convert a racemate into diastereomers that can be separated. Classic resolution forms diastereomeric salts with a chiral acid or base (e.g. tartaric acid derivatives, mandelic acid) and crystallizes one. Kinetic resolution uses an enzyme or chiral catalyst that reacts faster with one enantiomer (maximum 50% yield of each).
- **Chiral chromatography**: preparative HPLC or SFC on chiral stationary phases (polysaccharide-based columns are workhorses).
- **Asymmetric synthesis**: chiral catalysts or auxiliaries create the desired centre directly, e.g. asymmetric hydrogenation.

Pasteur's 1848 hand-sorting of sodium ammonium tartrate crystals worked because that salt crystallizes as a **conglomerate** (separate crystals of each enantiomer), which is unusual; most racemates crystallize as a **racemic compound** with both enantiomers in one lattice.
levels.phd:
The thermodynamics of racemates explain many process-chemistry decisions. Roughly 90% of crystalline racemates are **racemic compounds** (true 1:1 co-crystals), a small fraction are **conglomerates** (mechanical mixtures of homochiral crystals), and some form **pseudoracemates** (solid solutions). Binary melting-point phase diagrams distinguish them: a conglomerate shows a single eutectic at the racemic composition, a racemic compound shows two eutectics flanking the racemate. This determines whether preferential crystallization is possible (conglomerates only) and why an enantioenriched sample can crystallize with lower ee than its mother liquor, or the reverse.

**Self-disproportionation of enantiomers** means that achiral processes such as sublimation, achiral chromatography or crystallization can partially separate enantioenriched mixtures. Always measure ee on the bulk, not on one fraction.

**Dynamic processes** change the limits. Dynamic kinetic resolution couples fast in situ racemization of the substrate with a selective reaction, allowing theoretical yields up to 100% of one enantiomer. Crystallization-induced diastereomer transformation does the same for epimerizable diastereomeric salts.

In vivo, enantiomers can interconvert. Thalidomide racemizes rapidly at physiological pH because the stereocentre bears an acidic proton alpha to the glutarimide carbonyl, so giving one enantiomer still exposes the patient to both. Ibuprofen undergoes unidirectional metabolic inversion: the (R)-enantiomer is converted to the active (S)-enantiomer via an acyl-CoA thioester and an epimerase. These cases show that the stereochemical identity of what is administered and what circulates can differ, and both must be measured with enantioselective bioanalysis.
levels.expert:
Decisions a development team faces with any chiral candidate:

**Racemate or single enantiomer?** Current regulatory expectation (FDA's 1992 policy statement and equivalent guidance elsewhere) is that stereoisomeric composition is known and justified. Developing a racemate requires characterizing both enantiomers' pharmacology, PK and toxicology, and showing interconversion behavior. In practice nearly all new chiral drugs are single isomers, unless the centre racemizes rapidly in vivo, in which case a racemate may be the honest choice.

**How to make it at scale?** Early discovery uses chiral SFC to separate milligram-to-gram amounts quickly. Development weighs classical resolution (cheap, robust, but discards half unless the wrong isomer can be recycled), enzymatic routes, and asymmetric catalysis. The 2001 Nobel Prize (Knowles, Noyori, Sharpless) honored asymmetric catalysis precisely because it changed how chiral drugs are manufactured.

**Specifications.** The unwanted enantiomer is controlled as an impurity, with a validated chiral method and limits justified by safety data. Diastereomers are controlled like any other related substance.

**Bioanalysis.** If inversion or racemization is plausible, plasma assays must be enantioselective; an achiral assay reporting 'total drug' can hide a mostly-inactive or toxic isomer.

Common errors: reporting ee from a crystallized fraction instead of the bulk; assuming a salt resolution product is enantiopure without checking the free base; and forgetting that a second stereocentre turns 'the other enantiomer' into a diastereomer with completely different physical properties, which is actually good news for purification.

keyPoints: Enantiomers are mirror images; diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not
Enantiomers have identical achiral properties; diastereomers differ physically
A racemate is a 50:50 mix of enantiomers, optically inactive
ee = % major − % minor
Single enantiomers come from chiral pool, resolution, chiral chromatography or asymmetric synthesis
Some drugs interconvert in vivo (thalidomide racemizes; R-ibuprofen inverts to S)

test.q: The enantiomer of an (R,S) compound is:
test.explain: An enantiomer inverts every stereocentre: (R,S) becomes (S,R). (R,R) and (S,S) are diastereomers of it.

test.q: Which property differs between two enantiomers?
choices: Boiling point in an achiral solvent
Melting point of the pure crystals
test.explain: Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light by equal amounts in opposite directions; achiral physical properties are identical.

test.q: Diastereomers can usually be separated by:
choices: Chiral HPLC, as achiral phases fail to resolve them
Distillation, since diastereomers differ in mass
test.explain: Diastereomers have different physical properties, so ordinary methods work.

test.q: A 50:50 mixture of two enantiomers is called a ___.
test.explain: A racemate (rac or ±) has no net optical rotation.

test.q: A sample contains 80% of the R enantiomer and 20% of the S. What is its enantiomeric excess (in %, number only)?
Diastereomers that differ at exactly one stereocentre are called:
test.explain: Epimers differ at one centre, e.g. glucose and galactose at C4.

test.q: Classical resolution of a racemic amine typically uses:
choices: A chiral acid to form diastereomeric salts
test.explain: A chiral acid (e.g. a tartaric acid derivative) forms two diastereomeric salts with different solubilities, so one crystallizes.

test.q: Are E and Z isomers of an alkene enantiomers or diastereomers?
test.explain: E/Z isomers are not mirror images, so they are diastereomers.

test.q: Why is giving pure (R)-thalidomide not a solution to its teratogenicity?
choices: The R form is itself the teratogenic enantiomer
The R form is not absorbed
test.explain: Thalidomide's stereocentre has an acidic proton next to a carbonyl, so it racemizes rapidly at physiological pH.

test.q: What is the maximum theoretical yield (%) of one enantiomer from a simple (non-dynamic) kinetic resolution of a racemate?
test.explain: Each enantiomer is half the material. Dynamic kinetic resolution, which racemizes the substrate in situ, can exceed this.

test.q: In the body, (R)-ibuprofen is:
test.explain: Ibuprofen undergoes unidirectional chiral inversion from R to the active S form.

kidTest.q: Mirror twin molecules, like left and right shoes, are called...
kidTest.explain: Mirror twins are enantiomers.

kidTest.q: Do mirror twins weigh the same?
kidTest.explain: Yes, mirror twins weigh the same and melt at the same heat.

kidTest.q: Look-alike molecules that are NOT mirror twins are like...
kidTest.explain: Diastereomers are like cousins: similar but different all over.

kidTest.q: A 50-50 mix of left and right twins is called a ___.
kidTest.explain: That 50-50 mix is a racemate.

kidTest.q: Why might scientists sort the twins in a medicine?
choices: To keep only the helpful one
kidTest.explain: Sometimes only one twin helps, so they keep that one.

advancedTest.q: Preferential crystallization (seeding a racemic solution with one enantiomer) works directly only for racemates that form:
advancedTest.explain: Only conglomerates crystallize as separate homochiral crystals that seeding can selectively grow.

advancedTest.q: Dynamic kinetic resolution can exceed 50% yield because:
choices: The slow-reacting enantiomer racemizes in situ and feeds the fast reaction
The catalyst irreversibly destroys the wrong enantiomer so the fast one exceeds 50%
Both enantiomers undergo the same rate of reaction, which creates a single product
Using a racemic catalyst doubles the amount of product from each substrate isomer
advancedTest.explain: Rapid substrate racemization continually replenishes the fast-reacting enantiomer.

advancedTest.q: A chiral drug candidate racemizes in plasma within minutes. The most defensible development strategy is often:
choices: Develop a single enantiomer anyway and ignore plasma
Develop the racemate and characterize both enantiomers
Use an achiral bioanalytical assay only
advancedTest.explain: If rapid interconversion makes a single isomer impossible to maintain in vivo, a characterized racemate is justified.

advancedTest.q: Which phenomenon allows achiral chromatography or sublimation to partially change the ee of an enantioenriched sample? (abbreviation or full name)
advancedTest.explain: SDE arises because homochiral and heterochiral associations differ, so achiral processes can fractionate ee.

lessons.title: Stereoselective drug action & chiral switches

levels.kid:
Think of a key and a lock. A key and its mirror-image key look almost the same, but only one turns the lock. Your body has lots of tiny locks.

Many medicines come as a mirror-twin pair. Often one twin is the good key that opens the lock and helps you. The other twin might do nothing, or it might open a different lock and cause a problem.

So scientists sometimes take an old medicine that was a mix of both twins and make a new version with only the good twin. That is called a **chiral switch**.
levels.hs:
Because receptors and enzymes are chiral, the two enantiomers of a drug can behave very differently. Scientists call the more active enantiomer the **eutomer** and the less active one the **distomer**. The ratio of their potencies is the **eudismic ratio**.

Why does this happen? The **three-point attachment model** says that if a drug touches its target at three spots, only one enantiomer can line up all three at once, just as only your right hand fits a right glove.

Examples:
- **Propranolol**: the (S)-enantiomer does almost all of the beta-blocking.
- **Ibuprofen**: (S) inhibits COX; the body converts much of the (R) form into (S).
- **Penicillamine**: only the D form is used as a medicine because the L form is toxic.

A **chiral switch** means redeveloping an existing racemic drug as a single enantiomer. Examples include esomeprazole (from omeprazole), escitalopram (from citalopram), levocetirizine (from cetirizine) and levofloxacin (from ofloxacin). Switches can give cleaner pharmacology or more predictable levels in the blood, but sometimes the benefit is small and the main effect is a new patent.
levels.college:
**Easson–Stedman (three-point) model**: an enantioselective interaction requires at least three points of differentiated contact between ligand and site. One enantiomer can satisfy all three; its mirror image can satisfy only two, unless the molecule reorients at an energy cost. This is a simplification (real binding is many contacts plus shape), but it captures why chiral recognition needs a chiral, three-dimensional partner.

**Pfeiffer's rule** (1956): the more potent the eutomer, the larger the eudismic ratio tends to be, because tighter, more specific binding is more sensitive to geometry.

**Patterns of enantiomer behavior:**
- One active, one inactive (escitalopram vs R-citalopram).
- Both active but at different targets. Labetalol has two stereocentres and four stereoisomers: the (R,R) isomer is mainly a beta blocker, while the (S,R) isomer is mainly an alpha-1 blocker.
- Different potencies at the same target (S-warfarin is several times more potent than R-warfarin).
- One responsible for toxicity.

**Stereoselective PK**: passive absorption is usually not stereoselective, but protein binding, transporter uptake, CYP metabolism and renal secretion can be. Warfarin's (S)-enantiomer is cleared mainly by CYP2C9 and the (R) by CYP3A4 and CYP1A2, so CYP2C9 genotype and inhibitors affect the more potent form. Omeprazole's (R)-enantiomer depends more on CYP2C19, so esomeprazole gives higher and less genotype-variable exposure.

**Chiral switch** value is judged case by case: improved selectivity or PK in some cases, little clinical difference in others.
levels.phd:
A rigorous view of stereoselectivity treats the drug–target complex: the two enantiomers form diastereomeric complexes whose binding free energies differ by ΔΔG = −RT ln(eudismic ratio). At body temperature a 100-fold eudismic ratio corresponds to roughly 12 kJ/mol, comparable to one or two good hydrogen bonds or the burial of a well-placed methyl group. Small chiral molecules with one stereocentre bound by a hydrophobic surface can show modest ratios, while rigid ligands with polar contacts on both sides of the centre often show ratios above 100.

Stereoselectivity is not a single number for a drug. It can invert between targets (one enantiomer preferring receptor A, the other receptor B), between species (orthologous binding sites differ), and between pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics. Net in vivo selectivity combines intrinsic affinity, stereoselective clearance and interconversion. A distomer with slower clearance can accumulate and contribute to effects or toxicity even if it is weak in vitro.

The chiral switch record is instructive:

- Successes with mechanistic rationale: esomeprazole (metabolic), levofloxacin (the S-enantiomer carries nearly all antibacterial activity, so the same effect needs less total drug load).
- Failures that taught caution: dilevalol, the (R,R) isomer of labetalol, was withdrawn in the few markets where it launched because of hepatotoxicity not obvious from the racemate's record; development of (R)-fluoxetine was stopped because of QT prolongation. Removing one enantiomer changes the exposure pattern of the other, and the racemate's safety history does not automatically transfer.

These cases support the modern rule: characterize each stereoisomer as a separate drug before deciding.
levels.expert:
How senior people think about stereoselectivity in a project:

- **Test both enantiomers early.** Separating a racemic hit by chiral SFC and testing both isomers is cheap. A large eudismic ratio is good evidence of a specific, structured binding mode; a ratio near 1 suggests nonspecific, lipophilic or aggregation-driven activity. It is one of the quickest sanity checks on a hit.
- **Use the distomer as a control.** A near-identical inactive enantiomer is the best negative control for cellular and in vivo experiments, because it shares physical properties, permeability and much off-target liability. If the 'inactive' enantiomer still produces the phenotype, the phenotype probably is not on-target.
- **Profile both for safety.** hERG, CYP inhibition and off-target panels can show opposite stereopreferences. The distomer is still an impurity and a possible metabolite, so its liabilities matter.
- **Watch PK as well as potency.** Stereoselective metabolism, polymorphic CYPs (2C9, 2C19, 2D6) and in vivo inversion change what the patient is exposed to. Plasma assays should be enantioselective until interconversion is excluded.

In the clinic, chiral-switch drugs are often prescribed interchangeably with the racemate, and the evidence of superiority varies. Judging a switch means asking what problem the single enantiomer solved: a real PK or selectivity gain, or mainly a commercial one. Answering that well requires understanding the exact pharmacology of each isomer, which is why stereochemistry stays relevant at the bedside and not only at the bench.

keyPoints: Eutomer = more active enantiomer; distomer = less active
Eudismic ratio = eutomer potency / distomer potency
Three-point attachment explains why chiral targets tell enantiomers apart
Enantiomers can differ in potency, target, metabolism and toxicity
Chiral switch = redeveloping a racemate as a single enantiomer (e.g. esomeprazole, escitalopram)
Labetalol: (R,R) beta blockade, (S,R) alpha-1 blockade

test.q: The more pharmacologically active enantiomer is called the:
test.explain: Eutomer = the 'good' (more active) enantiomer; distomer = less active.

test.q: The Easson–Stedman model proposes that enantioselective binding requires at least:
test.explain: With three differentiated contacts, only one enantiomer can satisfy all simultaneously.

test.q: Esomeprazole is the single enantiomer of:
test.explain: Esomeprazole is (S)-omeprazole, a classic chiral switch.

test.q: The ratio of eutomer potency to distomer potency is the ___ ratio.
test.explain: Eudismic ratio quantifies stereoselectivity.

test.q: Which enantiomer of propranolol is responsible for most beta blockade?
test.explain: (S)-propranolol is roughly 100 times more potent at beta receptors than (R).

test.q: Labetalol's (S,R) isomer mainly acts as:
test.explain: (S,R)-labetalol contributes alpha-1 blockade; (R,R) contributes beta blockade.

test.q: Which form of penicillamine (D or L) is used as a medicine?
test.explain: D-penicillamine is the therapeutic form; the L form is toxic.

test.q: Pfeiffer's rule states that:
choices: Both enantiomers tend to have equal receptor potency in a chiral binding pocket
A racemate tends to be safer than either of its pure enantiomer components
The less potent distomer is necessarily toxic because of its stereochemical label
The more potent the eutomer, the greater the eudismic ratio tends to be
test.explain: Tighter, more specific binding tends to be more stereosensitive.

test.q: S-warfarin is cleared mainly by which enzyme?
test.explain: CYP2C9 clears the more potent S-enantiomer, so CYP2C9 variants and inhibitors matter a lot for warfarin.

test.q: Redeveloping a racemic drug as a single enantiomer is called a chiral ___.
test.explain: Examples: escitalopram, levocetirizine, levofloxacin, esomeprazole.

test.q: Why can a chiral switch fail to improve on the racemate?
choices: The eutomer and distomer acquire opposite formal charges at physiological pH, cancelling selectivity
Enantiomers bind chiral targets identically, so a pure isomer behaves just like the racemate
Regulators bar single-isomer drugs once a racemic drug with the same formula has been marketed
The distomer may contribute little, so removing it changes little; or the eutomer alone may reveal new toxicity
test.explain: Benefits depend on what the distomer actually did. Dilevalol and R-fluoxetine show that single isomers can bring new problems.

kidTest.q: Only one key opens a lock. Medicines work a bit like...
kidTest.explain: Medicines are like keys for tiny locks in your body.

kidTest.q: If a medicine has mirror twins, are both always helpful?
choices: Yes, both twins work the same
kidTest.explain: Often only one twin is the good key.

kidTest.q: Making an old mix medicine with only the good twin is called a...
kidTest.explain: That's a chiral switch.

kidTest.q: The good twin opens the ___ and helps you.
kidTest.explain: The right key opens the lock.

kidTest.q: What might the other twin do?
choices: Turn into gold coins for you
Help even more than the first twin
Nothing, or open a different lock
kidTest.explain: It might do nothing or cause a different effect.

advancedTest.q: At 37 °C, a 100-fold eudismic ratio corresponds to a binding free-energy difference of about how many kJ/mol? (whole number)
advancedTest.explain: ΔΔG = RT ln(100) ≈ 2.58 kJ/mol × 4.6 ≈ 11.9 kJ/mol.

advancedTest.q: A racemic hit shows a eudismic ratio near 1 across several assays. The most likely interpretation is:
choices: Nonspecific or aggregation-driven activity, or a binding mode insensitive to the stereocentre
The assay must be highly enantioselective, because both isomers yielded equal effects
The hit must have a rigid, stereospecific binding pose with strong contacts at the chiral center
The compound is achiral despite having two isolated enantiomeric samples
advancedTest.explain: Specific, structured binding usually discriminates enantiomers; a ratio near 1 is a warning sign or shows the centre is solvent-exposed.

advancedTest.q: Why is the distomer an excellent negative control in cell experiments?
choices: It binds the target more tightly but has the same permeability as the eutomer
It is usually more toxic, so it reveals off-target cell death at lower doses
Its charge differs from the eutomer's, which alters uptake into the cells under study
It shares physicochemical properties and permeability with the eutomer but lacks on-target activity
advancedTest.explain: Same lipophilicity, solubility and permeability: differences in phenotype then point to on-target action.

advancedTest.q: Development of dilevalol, the (R,R) isomer of labetalol, was halted mainly because of:
advancedTest.explain: Dilevalol caused liver toxicity, showing that a single isomer's safety cannot be assumed from the racemate.

lessons.title: Conformations & ring flips

levels.kid:
Molecules are not stiff like rocks. Many parts can twist and turn, like your arms can wave around while you stay the same person. Each new pose is called a **conformation**.

Some rings of atoms are shaped like a little beach chair. The chair can flip, like flipping a pool float over. When it flips, the parts sticking up go out to the side, and the parts out to the side go up.

A medicine might have to bend into just the right pose to fit its lock. If it is too wiggly, it wastes time trying poses. So scientists sometimes make medicines a bit stiffer so they hold the right pose.
levels.hs:
A **conformation** is one 3D shape a molecule can take by rotating around single bonds. Changing conformation does not break any bonds, so conformers interconvert quickly, unlike enantiomers.

Looking down a C–C bond (a **Newman projection**), groups can be **staggered** (spread out, lower energy) or **eclipsed** (lined up, higher energy because electron clouds crowd each other). In butane, the **anti** conformation (the two methyls opposite) is the most stable; **gauche** (60° apart) is a little higher in energy.

Cyclohexane rings are not flat. They adopt a **chair** shape that removes almost all strain. Each carbon has one **axial** position (pointing straight up or down) and one **equatorial** position (pointing outward). A **ring flip** converts the chair into the other chair, and every axial group becomes equatorial and vice versa. Large groups prefer equatorial, because axial groups bump into other axial hydrogens on the same side (**1,3-diaxial interactions**).

For drugs, this matters because a molecule must adopt a particular **bioactive conformation** to fit its target. Flexible molecules pay an energy cost to freeze into that shape.
levels.college:
**Torsional analysis.** Rotation about single bonds is not free: ethane has a barrier of about 12 kJ/mol between staggered and eclipsed forms (torsional strain from eclipsing bonds). In butane, the gauche conformer lies roughly 3.8 kJ/mol above anti because of steric interaction between the methyl groups. At room temperature these barriers are crossed billions of times per second.

**Cyclohexane.** The chair has no angle strain and all bonds staggered. The ring flip passes through half-chair and twist-boat forms with a barrier near 45 kJ/mol, so it is fast at room temperature (on the order of 10^5 flips per second). Substituent preference is quantified by **A-values**, the free-energy difference between axial and equatorial: methyl about 7 kJ/mol, tert-butyl so large (over 20 kJ/mol) that it effectively locks the ring with tBu equatorial. In cis- and trans-disubstituted rings, you analyze both chairs and pick the one with more large groups equatorial.

**Other drug-relevant conformational facts:**
- **Amide bonds** are planar due to resonance, with a high rotational barrier, so cis/trans amide isomers interconvert slowly. Most amides are trans; tertiary amides such as proline's show substantial cis populations.
- **Biaryls** twist to avoid ortho clashes; ortho substituents increase the twist and can create atropisomers.
- **Saturated heterocycles** (piperidine, morpholine, piperazine) also adopt chairs, and the orientation of N-substituents affects binding.

**Bioactive conformation** is the shape bound to the target. It is usually close to, but not necessarily at, the global energy minimum.
levels.phd:
Binding thermodynamics treat flexibility explicitly. The observed affinity reflects the free energy of the bound complex minus the free energy of the unbound ensemble. If the bioactive conformer represents only a small fraction of the solution ensemble, the ligand pays a **conformational penalty**: ΔG_conf = −RT ln(fraction in bioactive conformation), plus enthalpic strain if the bound geometry is distorted from a local minimum. Analyses of crystal structures suggest most ligands bind within a modest strain window, while large strain energies often signal modelling errors.

Freezing rotatable bonds also costs conformational entropy, so each restricted rotor can contribute to affinity if the ligand is pre-organized correctly. This is the logic of **conformational restriction**: ring closure, macrocyclization, introducing a double bond or amide, or adding substituents that bias torsions. Done well, potency and selectivity rise together; done badly, the locked conformer cannot fit at all, which itself is informative about the bioactive shape.

Stereoelectronic effects bias conformations beyond sterics. The **anomeric effect** (an electronegative substituent at C1 of a pyranose preferring axial, rationalized by n→σ* donation) and the **gauche effect** (1,2-difluoroethane prefers gauche) are used deliberately; a fluorine placed beta to a protonated amine favors a gauche arrangement through charge–dipole interactions, which can rigidify a side chain.

The 'magic methyl' phenomenon, where adding one methyl raises potency more than tenfold, frequently results from conformational biasing: an ortho methyl on an aryl amide or biaryl shifts the torsional distribution toward the bioactive conformer, and a methyl on a piperidine can enforce an axial or equatorial preference. The hydrophobic contact itself is often a smaller contributor.
levels.expert:
Conformation is where medicinal chemistry intuition turns into design. Practical habits:

- **Read the structure biology carefully.** A co-crystal structure gives one bound conformation. Compare it with the ligand's low-energy conformers (computed, or from small-molecule crystal structures in the Cambridge Structural Database). If the bound torsions are rare in the database, the ligand is strained, and a modification that relieves strain is an obvious move.
- **Use rings and substituents to pre-organize.** Linking two parts of a flexible lead into a ring, or adding an ortho substituent to set a biaryl or aryl-amide twist, is a common route to large potency gains and better selectivity, because off-targets may require other shapes.
- **Mind properties.** Rigidification often lowers rotatable bond count and can improve oral absorption, but adding rings increases molecular weight and lipophilicity. Track lipophilic efficiency, not just potency.
- **Watch for slow equilibria.** Tertiary amide cis/trans rotamers, atropisomers and macrocycle conformers can show up as doubled peaks in NMR or HPLC. Do not mistake them for impurities, and do not let them become uncontrolled isomers in a drug substance.
- **Intramolecular hydrogen bonds** can create 'chameleonic' molecules that fold to hide polar groups in membranes and unfold in water, which helps explain the permeability of some large drugs beyond rule-of-five space.

The same ideas inform molecular pharmacology: agonists and antagonists can bind the same receptor in different conformations and stabilize different receptor conformations. A ligand's shape, and the shape it imposes, is ultimately the message it sends.

keyPoints: Conformers interconvert by rotation about single bonds without breaking bonds
Staggered is lower energy than eclipsed; anti butane is more stable than gauche
Cyclohexane chair: axial vs equatorial positions; ring flip swaps them
Bulky groups prefer equatorial (avoiding 1,3-diaxial strain); tert-butyl locks the ring
Drugs must adopt a bioactive conformation; flexibility carries an energy cost
Conformational restriction can raise potency and selectivity

test.q: Conformers differ from each other by:
test.explain: Conformations interconvert by rotation; no bonds break.

test.q: Which conformation of butane is the most stable?
test.explain: Anti places the two methyls 180° apart, minimizing steric and torsional strain.

test.q: In a cyclohexane chair, positions pointing straight up or down are called ___.
test.explain: Axial bonds are parallel to the ring axis; equatorial bonds point outward around the ring.

test.q: A ring flip in cyclohexane converts:
choices: Axial groups to equatorial and equatorial to axial
A chair ring into a permanently flat benzene-like structure
A cis arrangement into trans without breaking bonds
An R stereocentre into S without changing its bonds
test.explain: A ring flip swaps axial and equatorial; cis/trans relationships are unchanged.

test.q: A large substituent on cyclohexane prefers the equatorial position mainly to avoid:
test.explain: Axial groups clash with the axial hydrogens two carbons away on the same face.

test.q: Which substituent effectively locks a cyclohexane ring with it equatorial: methyl or tert-butyl?
test.explain: tert-Butyl's very large A-value makes the axial conformer essentially unpopulated.

test.q: Why does an amide C–N bond rotate slowly compared with a C–C single bond?
choices: The C–N bond is a full triple bond in amides
Water hydrogen bonds alone freeze the C–N bond
Resonance gives it partial double-bond character
Heavy nitrogen atoms physically prevent rotation
test.explain: Delocalization of the N lone pair into C=O makes the C–N bond partially double and planar.

test.q: The 3D shape a drug adopts when bound to its target is the ___ conformation.
test.explain: The bioactive conformation may differ from the lowest-energy conformation in solution.

test.q: Linking two parts of a flexible molecule into a ring to hold the bioactive shape is called:
test.explain: Conformational restriction reduces the entropic and conformational cost of binding if the right shape is locked.

test.q: Staggered conformations are lower in energy than eclipsed ones because:
choices: The staggered bonds can form new hydrogen bonds to their nearest carbon substituents
Eclipsed bonds create ring strain even in an open-chain alkane
The staggered form contains fewer C–C bonds and is therefore more stable
Eclipsed bonds have torsional strain from crowded electron clouds
test.explain: Eclipsing bonds causes torsional (Pitzer) strain.

test.q: What is the most stable conformation of cyclohexane called? (one word)
test.explain: The chair has near-ideal angles and fully staggered bonds.

kidTest.q: A molecule twisting into a new pose is called a...
kidTest.explain: Each pose is a conformation.

kidTest.q: Some rings of atoms are shaped like a...
kidTest.explain: Cyclohexane looks like a chair.

kidTest.q: When the chair flips, the parts sticking up...
kidTest.explain: Up becomes sideways and sideways becomes up.

kidTest.q: A medicine has to bend into the right ___ to fit its lock.
kidTest.explain: It needs the right pose (shape).

kidTest.q: Why make a medicine a bit stiffer?
choices: So it holds the right pose
kidTest.explain: A stiffer medicine holds the right pose and fits better.

advancedTest.q: If only 1% of a ligand's solution ensemble is in the bioactive conformation, about how many kJ/mol is the conformational penalty at 25 °C? (whole number)
An ortho methyl added to an aryl amide raises potency 30-fold, yet the methyl is solvent-exposed in the crystal structure. The most likely explanation is:
choices: Conformational biasing toward the bioactive torsion
New methyl–protein hydrophobic contacts outside the pocket
Methylation of the amide nitrogen into an ammonium salt
advancedTest.explain: The 'magic methyl' effect frequently comes from pre-organizing the ligand rather than from direct contact.

advancedTest.q: The anomeric effect favors an electronegative substituent at C1 of a pyranose being:
advancedTest.explain: Axial preference is rationalized by n(O)→σ*(C–X) hyperconjugation.

advancedTest.q: Doubled peaks in the NMR of a pure tertiary amide most likely reflect:
choices: Fast exchange of E and Z carbonyl isomers
Two hydrolysis impurities from the amide
Slow inversion at a carbonyl oxygen atom
advancedTest.explain: Tertiary amides rotate slowly on the NMR timescale, giving distinct rotamer signals.
